newsitem.title: GERMANY: Allianz drives to mitigate Holocaust PR threat. [CORRECTED 09:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Allianz drives to mitigate Holocaust PR threat. [CORRECTED 09:40 GMT]

text.p: A week into Allianz AG Holding's Holocaust telephone hotline service, part of the giant German insurer's bid to help descendants of Nazi victims track down missing assets, an odd calm has descended.
Hours go by without a single call, hotline organiser Gesine Lemke says, and those that do come through are more often than not from curious Allianz staff or reporters testing the system.

Of some 200 inquiries processed so far, only 13 were serious queries and only one -- from a Swiss man seeking to claim on a life insurance policy taken out by his long dead uncle -- yielded enough information to warrant more research.

But Allianz, acutely sensitive about the history of Nazi collaboration it shares with all major German corporates, remains on red alert following a massive U.S. lawsuit last month accusing it and six other insurance firms of cheating Holocaust victims of billions of dollars.
"A good reputation is a business asset," said spokesman Emilio Galli-Zugaro. "The value of Allianz's credibility cannot be measured in advance, but it can be measured in retrospect."

The suit, which lawyers say could be brought by up to 10,000 people, charges insurers with concealing or converting the cash value and proceeds of insurance policies sold before 1946 to mainly Jewish victims of Nazi persecution.
ALLIANZ ASSERTS BULK OF NAZI ERA CLAIMS SETTLED
It is not at all clear what kind of damages Allianz may face as a result of this suit and for the moment, the company does not even wish to speculate on any potential cost.
What it does want to do, however, is support its assertion that the bulk of claims against it from the Nazi era have already been settled and it has gone into public relations overdrive to do so.
"Our strategy is, before we go to any kind of court case, to show everything, to lay everything open," Galli-Zugaro said.

As well as the 24-hour hotline, which is multi-lingual and is supplemented by a counterpart in the United States, Allianz has hired auditing firm Arthur Andersen to assess some 800,000 files surviving from the Holocaust era.

Employees have received advice and information to help them parry questions from friends and acquaintances and press officers are constantly on call, in a drive whose administrative costs so far have exceeded 10 million marks ($5.8 million).

Even before the lawsuit began, Allianz had commissioned a team of U.S. historians to write an independent account of its activities under Hitler, during which it insists Jewish insurance assets were seized by the government and thus benefited only the Nazi regime, not the company.

The clarification task is likely to be a tough one. Many of Allianz's files were destroyed in the war. Others were seized by the East German communist government or simply cleared out over the years. And those that remain are organised by policy number, not by name.

Seven years after Allianz began to assemble its historical documents in the cellar of its Munich headquarters, its archive is still cluttered in a space no larger than a small schoolroom, with large clumps of papers yet to be organised.

"We know, for example, that Allianz did not actively oppose the Nazi government and that the company was forced to conduct its business under the same harsh restrictions imposed on all German companies by the Nazi regime," Allianz chairman Henning Schulte-Noelle wrote in a letter to employees.

"We also know that Allianz has in recent decades received a limited number of individual claims from Holocaust survivors or their families. Where these proved to be legitimate, the claims were paid," he continued.

"Each case would have been as different as the personal histories of those who filed them. This reality remains unchanged to this day. Also unchanged is the fact that Allianz will continue to review individual claims as they are filed and that all legitimate claims will be paid."
LEGAL ACCOUNTABILITY IS MURKY
Allianz's legal accountability for payouts is murky.
"As far as I am aware, we have no legal responsibility at all to act, but we feel we have a moral and a political responsibility to co-operate," said Galli-Zugaro.

Galli-Zugaro says records have been found of some 3,000 claims against Allianz under a 1956-1969 German law for the compensation of victims of National Socialist persecution but the company expects to uncover considerably more.
(Corrects to make clear that the 3,000 figure refers only to claims found so far, not to the total number in existence).

There are no plans to reinstate this law, which processed four to five million applications in all, despite sporadic complaints that residents of communist countries missed out on information on the scheme and the 1969 deadline.

That leaves an uncertain legal field for Allianz, whose Italian unit RAS and Austrian unit Wiener Allianz are also named in the suit along with Assicurazioni Generali S.p.A. of Trieste, Italy, Der Anker Allgemeine Versicherungs AG of Vienna, A.G.F. Assurances Generales de France (AGF) of Paris and Bavarian Reinsurance Co of Munich.
Meanwhile the Holocaust hotline team continues its work at a location kept secret because of fears of right-wing attacks.
While between six and eight staff manned the lines at the start, that has been reduced to two to three per shift now and will be cut back further, Lemke said.
The work, while delicate, has so far proved less traumatic than expected. Operators had feared being confronted with abuse, threats, or tears but said callers have been calm and business-like.
"No-one seems to want to start to tell their whole story over the telephone, which I find totally natural," Lemke said. "I wouldn't do it either." ($1 = 1.716 German Marks)
